a.summary: Removing the deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)` will not break callers — it will silently rebind `tx.sign(list)` to the by-key `sign(Collection<Signer>)`, flipping positional signing to key-matched signing with no compile error.
a.failure_scenario: Consumer code today: `List<Signer> signers = List.of(feePayer, authority); tx.sign(signers);` binds to `sign(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:784) and signs positionally. That method is now `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)`. When it is removed, `sign(Collection<Signer>)` (Transaction.java:773) is still applicable to a `List`, so the exact same source keeps compiling and now validates and signs by public key. A caller who deliberately relied on positional order — for example signing a message whose slot 0 signer is not the first element, which the deprecated overload permitted — either gets signatures in different slots or a new `IllegalArgumentException` at runtime for an assignment that used to succeed. This is the single most-used signing entry point, and it is the only one of the nine deprecated members with a silently-absorbing sibling: `sign(byte[], SequencedCollection)`, `sign(String, SequencedCollection)`, all three `signAndBase64Encode(*, SequencedCollection)` forms and the three deprecated statics have no `Collection` counterpart, so those call sites would fail to compile at removal, which is the behaviour `forRemoval` normally advertises.

b.summary: Removing the deprecated positional `sign(SequencedCollection)` will silently rebind every existing `tx.sign(someList)` call site to the by-key `sign(Collection)`, changing which signer fills which slot with no compile error and no warning in MIGRATION.md.
b.failure_scenario: A consumer today writes `List<Signer> signers = List.of(authority, feePayer); tx.sign(signers);`. Java binds that to `sign(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:784) and signs positionally: `authority` fills slot 0, `feePayer` fills slot 1 — the exact behaviour the new test `aListSelectsPositionalOrByKeySigningByName` pins for `signInOrder(reversed)`. Once that overload is removed (it is `forRemoval = true`), the identical source still compiles, because `List` is a `Collection`, and now binds to `sign(Collection)` (Transaction.java:773), which signs by public key: `feePayer` fills slot 0, `authority` fills slot 1. The transaction still serializes, still has 64 non-zero bytes in every slot, and `getBase58Id()` still returns a signature — it is simply a different, silently re-assigned transaction id. Contrast `signAndBase64Encode(list)`, `sign(hash, list)` and `sign(base58Hash, list)`, which fail loudly at removal because no `Collection` sibling exists; `sign(list)` is the one call shape that rebinds instead of breaking.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.
